hints: Focus on what controls each mechanism, think about how many species are involved in the slow, rate-determining step.
Remember that primary halogenoalkanes like chloroethane form very unstable carbocations, while secondary ones can go either way.
Picture the one-step SN2 attack by $\text{CN}^-$ and work out the overall charge when nucleophile and leaving group are both partly bonded.
walkthrough:
**Recall what SN1 and SN2 really mean**

The numbers tell you the molecularity of the slow step. SN1 is unimolecular and SN2 is bimolecular.

SN1 slow step:
$$\text{R-X} \rightarrow \text{R}^+ + \text{X}^-$$
SN2 single step:
$$\text{Nu}^- + \text{R-X} \rightarrow [\text{Nu} \cdots \text{R} \cdots \text{X}]^- \rightarrow \text{R-Nu} + \text{X}^-$$

**Link structure to mechanism**

SN1 needs a stable carbocation, so tertiary halogenoalkanes favour SN1. Primary halogenoalkanes like chloroethane form a very unstable primary carbocation, so they favour SN2.

Secondary halogenoalkanes are in the middle, so they can react by either SN1 or SN2 depending on conditions.

**Check the SN2 transition state charge**

In the SN2 reaction with cyanide, $\text{CN}^-$ attacks carbon as $\text{X}^-$ starts to leave. For a brief moment both are partly bonded to carbon.

Transition state:
$$[\text{N} \equiv \text{C} \cdots \text{R} \cdots \text{X}]^-$$
The incoming $\text{CN}^-$ brings a negative charge which is still present in this short-lived arrangement, so the transition state is negatively charged.

options.A: Incorrect. Secondary halogenoalkanes can react by both SN1 and SN2. They are not restricted to SN2 only, the pathway depends on factors like the stability of the carbocation, the nucleophile and the solvent.
options.B: Incorrect. In SN1 only the halogenoalkane is involved in the initial slow step, which is heterolytic fission to form a carbocation. The cyanide ion only attacks in the second fast step, so rate = k[halogenoalkane].
options.C: Incorrect. Chloroethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, is primary and would form a very unstable primary carbocation. It therefore reacts by SN2, where no full carbocation is formed.
options.D: Correct. The SN2 mechanism is concerted and goes through a single pentavalent transition state. With $\text{CN}^-$ as nucleophile, the complex $[\text{NC} \cdots \text{R} \cdots \text{X}]^-$ carries the negative charge from the cyanide ion and exists only very briefly.
